'''Donald Bruce Rubin''' (born December 22, 1943) is an American statistician, Emeritus Professor of Statistics at [[Harvard University]],<ref>{{cite web |url=https://statistics.fas.harvard.edu/people/donald-b-rubin/ |access-date=September 18, 2019|title=Donald B. Rubin|publisher=Harvard College}}</ref> where he chaired the department of statistics for 13 years.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://statistics.fas.harvard.edu/files/statistics/files/short_1_paragraph_bio_march_2017.pdf|title=Donald B. Rubin|publisher= Harvard College| access-date=September 18, 2019}}</ref> He also works at [[Tsinghua University]] in China and at [[Temple University]] in Philadelphia.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://bulletin.imstat.org/2018/09/fox-school-temple-university-appoints-rubin-and-airoldi/ |title=Fox School, Temple University, appoints Rubin and Airoldi |work=IMS Bulletin |last1= |first1= |last2= |first2= |date=September 1, 2018 |publisher=[[Institute of Mathematical Statistics]] |access-date=October 23, 2018 |quote= |archive-date=May 4, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190504211429/http://bulletin.imstat.org/2018/09/fox-school-temple-university-appoints-rubin-and-airoldi/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

He is most well known for the [[Rubin causal model]], a set of methods designed for [[causal]] [[inference]] with [[observational data]], and for his methods for dealing with [[missing data]].

== Biography ==
Rubin was born in [[Washington, D.C.]] into a Jewish family of lawyers.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Fan|last1=Li|first2=Fabrizia|last2=Mealli|title=A Conversation with Donald B. Rubin|journal=[[Statistical Science]]|date=2014 |pages=439–457|volume=29|issue=3|doi=10.1214/14-STS489|arxiv=1404.1789|bibcode=2014arXiv1404.1789L|s2cid=58334768}}</ref> As an undergraduate Rubin attended the accelerated [[Princeton University]] [[PhD]] program where he was one of a cohort of 20 students mentored by the [[John Archibald Wheeler|physicist John Wheeler]] (the intention of the program was to confer degrees within 5 years of [[freshman]] [[matriculation]]).  He switched to [[psychology]] and graduated in 1965.  He began graduate school in psychology at Harvard with a [[National Science Foundation]] fellowship, but because his statistics background was considered insufficient, he was asked to take introductory statistics courses.

Rubin became a PhD student again, this time in statistics under [[William Gemmell Cochran|William Cochran]] at the Harvard Statistics Department.  After graduating from Harvard in 1970, he began working  at the [[Educational Testing Service]] in 1971, and served as a visiting faculty member at [[Princeton University|Princeton]]'s new statistics department.  He published his major papers on the [[Rubin causal model]] in 1974–1980, seminal papers on [[propensity score matching]] in the early 1980s with [[Paul R. Rosenbaum|Paul Rosenbaum]], and a textbook on the subject with Nobel prize winning econometrician [[Guido Imbens]] in 2015.<ref name=cambridge-imbens-rubin>{{cite web|title=Causal Inference in Statistics, Social, and Biomedical Sciences|url=http://www.cambridge.org/er/academic/subjects/statistics-probability/statistical-theory-and-methods/causal-inference-statistics-social-and-biomedical-sciences-introduction|website=Cambridge University Press|accessdate=24 February 2015}}</ref>

In 1977 he was elected as a [[Fellow of the American Statistical Association]].<ref>[http://www.amstat.org/awards/fellowslist.cfm Fellows of the ASA] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160616161612/https://www.amstat.org/awards/fellowslist.cfm |date=2016-06-16 }}, accessed 2016-08-20.</ref> In 2007, Rubin was awarded the [[Snedecor Award|George W. Snedecor Award]] by the [[Committee of Presidents of Statistical Societies]].<ref>{{cite web | title=George W. Snedecor Award | website=Committee of Presidents of Statistical Societies| url=https://community.amstat.org/copss/awards/snedecor }}</ref>
